newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Buba official sees few southerners at start of EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buba official sees few southerners at start of EMU.

text.p: Southern nations as a group could not expect to be included if the European currency union is to start on time by the year 2000, although some could perhaps be in the first batch, a senior Bundesbank official said on Wednesday.

Hans-Juergen Koebnick, a Bundesbank council member, did not say which countries were likely to be excluded or comment directly on doubts about Italy's ability to join, expressed but later retracted by French President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday in controversial remarks that triggered a Franco-Italian diplomatic spat.

Koebnick also suggested that all nations should consider postponing the launch date by one or two years to give all members, including the group's leaders Germany and France, more time to prepare adequately for the union.

"A conditioned waiting for the currency union would not be a catastrophe," Koebnick said, explaining that the changes that need to be implemented in order to meet monetary union criteria were so massive that nations could use more time to prepare.

Germany is expected this year to miss the key criteria which state that budget deficits and government debt must not exceed three percent and 60 percent of GDP respectively. But Bonn officials insist that the the union will start on time.
Koebnick told Reuters that the southern nations, as a group, did not stand a chance of making the grade needed to enter the currency union with Germany and France by the end of the decade.

If European policy makers insist on launching the currency union in 1999 and want the new currency, the Euro, to be strong, "then one cannot allow others to join...for example the entire Club Med group cannot join," Koebnick said in a reference to the Club Mediterreanee holiday camps that operate around the sunny shores of the Mediterranean.

He urged politicians to withstand the temptation to swing open the entry gate to unprepared nations. Letting in nations which could not muster the necessary fiscal credentials would result in a "foul compromise" which could threaten the currency union's long term viability, Koebnick said.
The French president's remarks helped fan a simmering row between fiscally stringent northern states in the European Union and southen nations seen by some as less disciplined.

But analysts said it would be wrong to say the Bundesbank, the champion of fiscal propriety, wanted to exclude all southern nations from the currency union as has been suggested by some European politicians.

The Bundesbank's main objective is to lay the groundwork for lasting price stability, and this can be achieved only if membership is limited to nations with low deficits and government debt, analysts said.

Koebnick said that progress in meeting the debt and deficit criteria among so-called Club Med nations has been very mixed, with Portugal making strides in the right direction while others have fared less well.

He said a smaller starting group, including Germany, France and probably the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Belgium, would not damage the currency union in the long run since surveys showed that about 13 of the total of the EU's 15 nations would be ready to join before the year 2002.
Even while some nations will remain on the periphery at the start, their consolidation efforts will be rewarded when markets will treat them as potential members, Koebnick said.
He added that the second group of nations would likely be able to join the currency union some two years after the union is launched.
Political leaders will determine in 1998 which nations will be eligible to join the monetary union after reviewing their 1997 economic data.

Echoing warnings by many of his Bundesbank colleagues, Koebnick argued against what he called a "foul compromises" to decide who will be able to join the currency union as nations failing to meet the stability criteria threaten the union's viability.
